question: Base freshness for implementation worktrees: the as-built pipeline (src/core/implementation.rs, verified v1.1) captures the connected checkout's committed LOCAL HEAD (branch name via `git symbolic-ref --short HEAD`, commit via `git rev-parse HEAD`) and cuts the ticket worktree from that commit — with no `git fetch` or `git pull` anywhere before or during worktree creation — then publishes with `gh pr create --base <captured branch name>`. Confirm this local-HEAD, no-remote-refresh base is AS-INTENDED (and should be documented as such), or rule for an optional refresh step before branching (update the local tracking branch from the remote first, or branch from the freshly fetched upstream commit).
reason: A checkout that trails its remote starts tickets from a stale base: the implementation compiles and verifies against outdated code, risking PRs that conflict with, duplicate, or silently diverge from upstream work, and local-only unpushed commits would ride along as part of the PR base. Settling before broader multi-repo use avoids retrofitting, and any fetch option is a deliberate departure from NFR-5's strictly-zero Packet-initiated network posture (admission of git-brokered remote traffic) that deserves an explicit ruling rather than quiet accretion.
evidence: Resolution outcome: Recorded and resolved CLR-019: refresh before implementing is mandatory, ruling D-30's fetch clause as unconditional. Your call matches the as-built pipeline, which now fetches origin/<base> into a Packet-private ref before every worktree — preferring the newer side of a fast-forward pair, refusing outright when local and remote have diverged, and never pulling into your checkout. Living modules already state this decision (D-30, D-22, 09-environment, 11-risks), so no spec rewrite is owed. One retained semantic: when your local branch is strictly ahead of origin, the worktree anchors to the local tip, so unpushed local commits can ride along as base ancestry — preserved deliberately rather than lost. If you ever want local-ahead refused too, that's a fresh change request.

question:

reason: Deprioritized by D-22's post-MVP phasing ruling (CLR-014 resolved): this no longer gates MVP planning or the §12 exit bar, and is now the lead design question of the post-MVP channel project proper — it decides what Packet becomes network-wise (a listener, a dialer, or a relay), scopes the NFR-5 attack surface before the channel ships, and fixes the transport-library and runtime choice against NFR-7's offline/minimal posture. Prefer the simplest viable topology: direct instance-to-instance, endpoints manually entered from git-remote host info first, LAN-scoped; defer relay/internet reach until a concrete off-site teammate need appears, keeping NFR-7's minimal offline posture intact.

Operator ruling in the CLR-015 conversation (Zachary Barno, seated per D-23): "can it just rely on the fact that they have access to the repo?" Read as the trust decision: channel authentication = repository access itself (being able to reach/clone/push the shared remote qualifies the peer); no separate accounts or credentials. Consequence recorded: the socket handshake must cryptographically demonstrate possession of that access at connect time; mechanism deliberately left to the channel project's design phase. Resolution outcome: Retried cleanly and D-32 now carries the full channel ruling: direct instance-to-instance WebSockets (instances listen and dial; no relay), endpoints manually entered from git-remote host info first, local-network reach for the first cut, and trust grounded in repository access, proved at connect time via the peer's git-derived identity - no accounts, no Packet-minted secrets. CLR-015 is resolved; only the concrete handshake mechanic remains, paired with CLR-016's writer model in the channel design phase. Decisions, scope, NFR-5, data model, architecture, and risks modules updated.

question: Exclusive-ownership assumption (CHG-004): cleanup resolves candidates solely from the task's recorded worktree/branch metadata and its documented sibling naming (`<key>`, `<key>-integration-<base[:12]>`, `packet/<key>`, `packet/integration/<key>/<base[:12]>`) inside `<checkout-parent>/.packet-worktrees/<project-slug>/`, assuming Packet exclusively owns that subtree for the connected project. Nothing found incidentally in the roots (other tools, another Packet instance, manual directories) is ever a candidate. Proposed enforcement: before removing, confirm each candidate is registered in `git worktree list` at the recorded path; any registration/path mismatch aborts that item with a diagnostic instead of removing.
reason: Makes 'never touches foreign checkouts' operable rather than aspirational: without the guard, a coincidental occupant of the worktrees roots could be swept by an otherwise harmless done step, and the operator has a history of manual passes sharing those roots.
recommendation: Adopt the record-only candidate rule plus the worktree-list path-match guard as written; reversible at story review.
evidence:
Record construction in src/core/implementation.rs: root = repo parent + .packet-worktrees + project slug; branch `packet/<key>`; integration sibling derived from the state.worktree file-name plus branch `packet/integration/<key>/<base[:12]>`. The feature's Decisions and Assumptions already assume exclusive ownership; this item converts it into an enforcement strategy. Resolvable from evidence at story-writing time; no user input needed.

Resolution outcome: Investigated CLR-027 read-only and it resolves: the exclusive-ownership assumption is operationally sound — Packet creates the worktrees root itself (src/core/implementation.rs:578–581), persisted Implementation records carry exact worktree paths and branches for the task and each per-(task,base) integration sibling (:23–29, :1215, :1221–1230), and task keys embed a 16-hex FNVA1A64 fingerprint so foreign name collisions are negligible. I confirmed the record-scoped candidate rule and adopted the proposed guard with sharpened edges: one parsed `git worktree list` snapshot per cleanup; per-candidate match of recorded path (lexically normalized) and recorded branch; mismatch or a present-but-unregistered directory aborts that item with a diagnostic and removes nothing; a gone registration with an absent directory degenerates to `git worktree prune` plus diagnostic (prune only strips missing-dir registrations). The codebase already uses the mirror idiom (identity-mismatch 'refusing to modify' guards at :715–722, :1274–1277), and no removal path exists yet, so the guard is additive. Change recorded in the CHG-004 spec (Desired Behavior, R4, Decisions, AC5); CLR-027 resolved. Remaining human item on this feature: CLR-026 (branch reclamation under squash).

question: "Divergent" operational definition for the CHG-004 R4 skip guard. Proposed deterministic predicate: a candidate worktree is removable only if `git status --porcelain` is empty AND its HEAD commit remains reachable from at least one surviving ref after branch handling (a kept-not-merged branch or a remote-tracking ref); "divergent" otherwise. Git's own refusal at `git worktree remove` (dirty, locked) remains the final guard — never `--force`. A candidate whose directory is already absent degenerates to registration pruning plus diagnostic and counts as handled for AC4.
reason: AC4 must simulate dirty and missing-directory states with a crisp, testable pass/fail predicate, and the predicate must not recompute ancestry (the ruling delegates to Git). Locking the wording now keeps the implementation stories mechanical rather than interpretive.
recommendation: Adopt the predicate as stated: clean status + post-branching reachability + Git refusal as final guard; missing directory degenerates to prune+diagnose, not failure.
evidence:
Feature R4/AC4; `git worktree remove` without `--force` refuses dirty worktrees natively; missing-directory states are realistic because the operator already ran a manual cleanup pass at the time of the ruling, which can strand registrations without directories. Agent-resolvable during story writing; recorded so the plan is auditable.

Resolution outcome: CLR-028 investigated read-only and resolved. Source verification: squash publication at implementation.rs:1294, containment reconfirmation at :1194 with delegation probes at :1202-1208, verified_head refusal idioms at :972-973 and :1377-1383, and still no worktree-removal or branch-deletion path anywhere in src/, so the guard is additive. The locked operative definition stands, formalised this turn: a candidate is removable iff CLEAN (empty git status --porcelain) AND HEAD-STABLE (HEAD equals the recorded verified_head) AND ANCHORED (a surviving ref under refs/heads|refs/remotes|refs/packet-* contains HEAD per Git-delegated probes, or its delivery is attested at that head) - 'divergent' is the negation, skipped with a specific diagnostic and no mutation. Git's unqualified-remove refusal (dirty/locked) is the final guard, never --force; an absent directory degenerates to prune-plus-diagnostic and counts as handled. Reachability alone would leak published worktrees under the squash regime, hence the attested-delivery arm; one new edge locked: an externally deleted branch ref under a live registration matches the exclusivity guard only at the exact recorded HEAD. AC4 is now a crisp S1-S8 pass/fail simulation set. Remaining CHG-004 item: CLR-026 (branch reclamation under squash, Review, provisional lean on the board). No reply needed.

question: Branch reclamation under squash (CHG-004 R3): auto-publication delivers the task as a SQUASH commit on the default branch (`git merge --squash` in the integration worktree), so the original `packet/<key>` commits are not ancestors of the published tip and `git branch -d` usually REFUSES to delete the task branch after confirmed publication. Strict R3 (ruling-faithful) keeps task branches — directories are reclaimed, but one local branch still accrues per finished task, which is half of the pain the operator reported. Option 1 — keep R3 strict to Git's `-d` (retain task branches that fail the ancestry check, record the refusal reason). Option 2 — treat the confirmed publication as the merge attestation for Packet-created task/integration branches: confirmed auto-publication (persisted candidate commit present in the remote default-branch history — a check the pipeline already performs for lost-push recovery) or a polled MERGED, combined with a clean worktree, authorizes branch deletion even where `-d` refuses on ancestry; strict `-d` still applies anywhere no such attestation exists.
reason: Decides whether R3 is genuinely effective and what the branch tests in AC5 assert. Option 1 risks the feature feeling inert on the branch axis (the operator's manual-pass habit persists); Option 2 deletes branches on a stronger operational attestation than raw ancestry but departs from the ruling's literal wording. Neither endangers work — the dirty/divergent rails stand — so this is a bookkeeping-aggressiveness ruling, best settled before stories hard-code branch handling.
recommendation: Provisional (board-reviewable): Option 2 for the attested cases — the published content demonstrably reached the remote default branch, and the ancestry check exists to protect unmerged work, of which there is none once publication is confirmed; keep strict `-d` everywhere no confirmed publication/MERGED attests (failed, attention, review states). Integration branches are unaffected either way: they fast-forward-push, so `-d` already accepts them.
evidence:
src/core/implementation.rs: auto-publish runs `merge --squash <task_head>` in the integration worktree then one atomic fast-forward push; the task branch `packet/<key>` is created at record construction and no branch-deletion path exists anywhere in implementation.rs / implementation_queue.rs / reconciliation.rs (read-only audit). `git branch -d` semantics: refuses unless the commit is an ancestor of the merge destination — a squash descendant is not. Operator pain statement: one pair of directories PLUS local branches per finished task; manual pass after every merge/PR.

Resolution outcome: Locked in: Option 2 (attested deletion) is the settled rule. The contract is already recorded in CHG-004 — R3, the Settled decision citing your delegations, and AC1/AC2/AC5 — so this turn only closes the ledger: CLR-026 is resolved, leaving CHG-004 with no open items and ready for the in-app "Approve feature for implementation" release. No reply needed.

question: Assume the time ledger is a dedicated git-backed artifact whose commit cadence Packet picks at task generation.
reason: NFR-1 demands git-backed truth while the per-turn checkpoint culture (FR-3) warns against history flooding from per-tick commits; a dedicated ledger artifact committed on coarse grains (session save, end of day, export) is the safe reversible default. Surfaced on the board so the assumption is visible and challengeable rather than buried in prose.
evidence:
Resolution outcome: CLR-032 investigated and resolved from repository evidence. Grounds: NFR-1 requires git-backed shared truth (module 06), FR-3 scopes exactly one git checkpoint per mutating planning turn and forbids checkpoints on no-op turns — the per-tick commit culture that flooding would come from. Module 07 shows the established store layout: durable facts live in dedicated slots under .kool-ade-packet/, applied atomically per NFR-2, with checkpoints subject-phrased per NFR-9. Synthesis recorded in AD-3 (now a reasoned agent determination, not an open bet): the time ledger is a dedicated git-backed artifact in the project store; its rows are written atomically to the file immediately (durability is in the file bytes, NFR-1 satisfied at commit time), while git commits fire only at coarse grains the ledger owner picks at task generation — candidate grains: session save/close, day rollover, period export. Event-granular commits are ruled out by FR-3; pure commit-per-export alone weakens restart recovery (weakened only slightly, since rows are in the file regardless). The choice of exact trigger set stays a task-generation detail, keeping the feature model-agnostic like its open capture decisions.

decision_brief.question: How should billable time get into the ledger?
decision_brief.whyNow: Everything downstream — the data model, the UI, the anti-inflation rule, and the acceptance criteria — forks on this choice, so the feature cannot leave Draft until it is settled.

recommendation.rationale: Deliberate start/stop gives defensible, dispute-proof hours with the least machinery, matching the stated aim of billing clients accurately in a single-seat desktop. Forgotten stops are the main residual risk and are mitigable with a reminder and visible open-interval state.

confidence.explanation: The accuracy-driven intent is clear from the request, but passive versus timer is partly a personal habit choice and the product documents offer no evidence of a preferred rhythm.

options.label: Passive foreground counting
options.summary: Wall-clock time is credited automatically while Packet is in front on a client’s workspace, with an idle threshold dropping unattended stretches.
benefits: No start/stop discipline required
Captures choppy focus naturally
costs: Idle-threshold tuning is itself an accuracy surface
Larger first slice: detection logic and tuning before any hours appear
risks: Overstatement of billed minutes if idle detection mistakes a step-away for work
consequences: Challenged hours require defending a heuristic
options.reversibility: Moderate: records stay auditable intervals, but switching later changes how past days are read.

options.label: Explicit start/stop timer per client
options.summary: The operator starts and stops a timer aimed at a client (optionally narrowed to a card); counted time is the union of deliberate intervals.
benefits: Every billed minute is intentional and defensible
Smallest credible first slice: start/end pairs
costs: Discipline required; forgotten stops need a reminder and visible open-interval state
risks: Left-running timers can overstate without the stop reminder
consequences: Off-app time is unrecorded unless logged afterwards
options.reversibility: High: intervals are self-describing; passive counting could be layered on later without rewriting history.

options.label: Retrospective log entries only
options.summary: Hours are keyed in after the fact at day or task granularity, with no live capture at all.
benefits: Zero runtime machinery
Flexibility for irregular schedules
costs: Memory-dependent; weakest link to billing accurately
risks: Entries blur the day and week boundaries they report on
consequences: Timesheets are reconstructions rather than measurements
options.reversibility: High: entries are discrete facts; live capture can be added later.

benefits: Picks the accuracy contract the operator stands behind with clients
Sets first-slice complexity and test surface
costs: Wrong pick means rebuilding the capture surface and re-learning a habit
risks: An underestimated idle or forgetfulness problem resurfaces as invoice disputes
ramifications: Determines what a billed minute means legally and practically for the operator
Shapes the fidelity rule R3 and AC1 concretely
decision_brief.reversibility: Records remain compatible across mechanisms (they all reduce to auditable intervals), so the choice can be relaxed or tightened later; the main cost is first implementations and early-formed habits.

decision_brief.question: The export period is now fixed: the calendar month, 1st through last. What form should the monthly report itself take — on-screen totals plus CSV export, printable summary, or on-screen totals only?
decision_brief.whyNow: The period is settled (calendar month, 1st through last), so R5 (export) and the reporting UI now depend only on the artefact form; settling it keeps the first slice from shipping a month-end report the operator never sends out.

recommendation.rationale: On-screen day/week/month totals serve everyday checking, and a CSV drops into whatever spreadsheet or invoicing tool the operator already uses at month-end, at the lowest cost of exactness.

confidence.explanation: CSV versatility is uncontested for month-end hand-offs, but the operator's downstream invoice tooling is unknown and they may prefer a ready-to-send document.

options.label: On-screen totals plus CSV export
options.summary: Per-client day/week totals on the board plus a CSV export of a chosen period, offering entry rows and client summaries.
benefits: Works with any downstream invoice tool
Exact by construction — the same sums the screen shows
costs: Minimal: one exporter and its round-trip test
risks: Essentially none; CSV is inert data
consequences: Invoice preparation becomes copy-from-Packet into existing flow
options.reversibility: High: more formats can be added later without touching the ledger.

options.label: Printable period summary
options.summary: A formatted document (print view or PDF) styled to drop straight into or alongside an invoice.
benefits: Near-final artefact in one click
Consistent professional presentation
costs: Layout and formatting care in the first slice
consequences: Editing happens in a document rather than a spreadsheet
options.reversibility: Moderate: regenerating past periods in a new layout is fine; edited copies already sent are not recalled.

options.label: On-screen totals only

costs: Hand transcription reintroduces the original inaccuracy

consequences: Packet advises the invoice but never evidences it
options.reversibility: High: exporting can be bolted on later.

question: Broken down 'by feature name': should each report line be titled by the planning feature the worked item traced to, falling back to the item's own title, then a 'General' catch-all for untitled time?
reason: The terse ruling fixes the form and the two breakdown axes but not the exact label chain, and the chain sets what invoice-bound names print on the month sheets. Settled as a reversible read-time derivation in F7 AD-9 (labels derive at render; no ledger rows are touched), and it should be confirmable or correctable from the first generated report sample. Does not gate tasks.
evidence:
Operator reply in this thread ('just markdown files for the month broken down by day and feature name') settles form and breakdown axes; AD-5 records the producing worker/session per interval and board items carry feature context, giving a render-time label chain to hang the assumption on.

Resolution outcome: CLR-033 settled as an agent assumption: the label chain is planning-feature display title → worked item's own title → "General", derived at render time with no ledger-row changes (AD-9). Grounding: Packet task tickets already carry an explicit "Feature:" traceability line tying each item to its planning feature, and AD-5 records the producing item per interval, so the chain hangs on existing durable links; AC3 keeps printed lines summing to on-screen totals.
